lesson.title: Link Adaptation: Squeezing Every Bit Out of a Changing Radio Channel
lesson.summary: Link adaptation continuously adjusts modulation and coding to match a wireless channel's current quality, trading throughput for robustness on the fly instead of locking every device into one fixed transmission scheme.
lesson.body:
A wireless medium is nothing like a copper cable: its quality changes constantly as a device moves, as obstacles come and go, and as other transmitters compete for the same spectrum. Link adaptation is the practice of adjusting how a transmitter encodes its signal, moment to moment, to match whatever quality that wireless medium currently offers, instead of picking one fixed scheme and living with the consequences.

The two parameters most commonly adjusted are the modulation scheme and the coding rate, together often summarized as an MCS, or modulation and coding scheme, index. Higher order modulation packs more bits into every symbol, for example 256 QAM encodes 8 bits per symbol compared to just 2 bits per symbol for QPSK, which means far higher throughput on the same amount of spectrum. The tradeoff is that higher order modulation packs its symbols closer together in signal space, so it takes very little noise to make the receiver mistake one symbol for another. A device with a strong, clean signal to a base station can safely use 256 QAM; a device near the edge of a cell with a noisy signal has to fall back to a more robust, lower throughput scheme like QPSK or 16 QAM just to keep its error rate acceptable.

The coding rate works alongside modulation to add redundancy that lets a receiver correct errors without asking for a retransmission. A lower coding rate adds more redundant bits and tolerates a noisier channel at the cost of throughput, while a higher coding rate carries more useful data per symbol but needs a cleaner channel to decode reliably. Link adaptation picks a combination of modulation and coding rate that maximizes throughput while keeping the resulting error rate within an acceptable target, and it reevaluates that choice continuously as conditions change.

In cellular networks, this process is usually called adaptive modulation and coding, and it depends on the device reporting a channel quality indicator, or CQI, back to the base station many times per second, based on measurements of the reference signals it receives; the base station uses that feedback to select an MCS for the next transmission. Wi Fi networks solve the same problem with rate adaptation algorithms running locally on the transmitter, such as Minstrel or the older ARF algorithm, which infer channel quality indirectly from whether recent transmissions succeeded or needed retries, since 802.11 does not always give a transmitter the kind of direct channel quality feedback that cellular networks do.

Link adaptation is what keeps both Wi Fi and cellular networks fast under good conditions and merely functional under bad ones, rather than forcing every device onto the lowest common denominator. It also interacts directly with handoff: a device whose channel quality has degraded enough that link adaptation keeps falling back to slower and slower schemes is often the same device a network will soon hand off to a stronger neighboring cell, since link adaptation can only compensate for a weak signal, not fix it.
